reviewEvidence.resolutionNote: Research-only reference media; never a production source. Independent production footage still requires genuine FHD or higher.
reviewEvidence.visualReviewMethod: Four sequential 3x4 contact sheets sampled every six seconds across the entire reference, plus a full-size frame at 00:30. Read visible English burned-in captions, motion list fields, grid demonstrations, pose specifications, comparison examples and concluding visuals.
reviewEvidence.limitations: Japanese automatic captions contain recognition errors, especially music-only montage stretches. English on-screen subtitles and diagrams corroborate the teaching claims. This is visual/transcript analysis, not a claim of real-time complete audio listening.

corrections.viewerUse: Personal production-specific quantity; omit if not necessary, never state it as a universal required count.

centralQuestion: How can the person planning a character communicate the intended movement clearly enough for animators to produce it?
thesis: Start with an explicit motion list and timing requirements, add visual pose references where they clarify intent, then let animators resolve the actual movement through iterative review while sharing the lessons across the team.
notTheTopic: A tutorial for a particular animation package
Simply collecting cool poses without a production specification
A claim that a detailed brief removes the animator's design work

claims: Animation refers here to how characters move.
The category discusses transferable production concepts rather than software-specific operations.
sections.observedVisuals: Title and presenter introduce the animation category before the episode begins.
sections.retainedTeaching: Define animation through a visible character changing posture over time before discussing specifications.
additionalPrerequisites: Distinguish a single pose from an animation over time.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Our neutral articulated character on the requested grid: show one held pose, then the same short movement; label pose versus animation.
sections.transitionToNext: A finished movement begins as someone else's intended action; the next question is how that intent reaches its animator.

claims: Character planning includes both the move and the intended impression of that move.
The planner needs to communicate the nuance to the animation team.
sections.observedVisuals: Inkling animation followed by a diagram connecting direction, documents and animators.
exampleRoles: A recognizable completed fighter establishes the desired result.
A handoff diagram introduces the specification as a communication tool.
sections.retainedTeaching: Use a concrete requested action to show why intent needs to become a shared specification.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Independent actual gameplay establishes a recognizable movement; our grid character then shows two interpretations of one vague request. Clearly label the latter as our illustrative comparison.
sections.transitionToNext: The first way to remove missing or ambiguous requirements is to enumerate the movements.

claims: Create a written inventory of the required animations.
Describe the intended movement in text.
Record animation duration and when an attack begins and ends.
Choose timings in relation to the game's back-and-forth interaction.
For repeatable idle or walking motions, identify looping or flexible-duration behavior rather than treating every entry as a fixed one-shot.
sections.observedVisuals: Motion spreadsheet is progressively magnified; attack timing columns are called out; Inkling side-smash motion appears on a grid with a frame counter and attack start/end labels.
exampleRoles: The spreadsheet makes the deliverable finite and inspectable.
The frame counter ties a written timing requirement to the visible attack.
Loop entries contrast repeating and one-shot motions.
sections.retainedTeaching: Keep the list-to-time-axis relationship rather than replacing it with a generic Animator tutorial.
additionalPrerequisites: Define frame as a sampled moment and specify playback rate before converting frame counts to seconds.
Distinguish the animation's total duration from its active attack interval.
Explain loop by showing the end reconnect to the start.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Own three-row motion list (idle, walk, attack) alongside the grid mannequin. Highlight a row while its motion runs. For an explicitly illustrative 60 fps example, a 12-frame interval represents 0.2 seconds; show the chosen attack interval as a bar without presenting it as a measurement of a commercial game.
sections.transitionToNext: The list establishes what and when; a visual pose reference establishes how the body should look.

claims: Use photographed articulated-figure poses to communicate essential idle, movement and attack shapes.
Pose the figure, photograph it, isolate its silhouette, adjust contrast and place it into a specification.
sections.observedVisuals: Physical poseable figure and a sequential pose/photo/cutout/contrast/spec-sheet process.
exampleRoles: A tangible reference removes ambiguity that text alone leaves.
The process turns a demonstration into a reusable production document.
sections.retainedTeaching: Retain the explicit sequence from reference pose to a readable specification; do not skip directly from an abstract idea to finished animation.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Capture our licensed articulated Unity character from a fixed grid camera; show the same silhouette as a pose thumbnail next to a short intention note. State that this is a digital stand-in for making a visual reference rather than a filmed physical figure.
sections.transitionToNext: Once the pose reference exists, compare the document with the movement that realizes it.

sections.role: Worked gallery: specification to realized animation
claims: A pose specification makes the intended movement concrete.
Different movement families require different poses, transitions and object relationships.
sections.observedVisuals: Alternating specification pages and finished animations on a visible coordinate grid, then side-by-side comparisons. The largely music-led gallery shows Inkling side/up smash, King K. Rool throws, Simon side smash/cross throw, Incineroar dodges, Joker side tilt/gun poses, Byleth smash attacks, Sephiroth idles and Pyra/Mythra taunts.
exampleRoles: Inkling: pose/weapon direction maps to an attack.
King K. Rool: interaction between two bodies for a throw.
Simon: long or thrown weapon trajectory adds a constraint.
Joker: repeated attack and weapon poses.
Byleth: distinct attack directions and weapon shapes.
Sephiroth: idle pose and silhouette matter without an attack.
Pyra/Mythra: gesture and character relationship communicate personality.
sections.retainedTeaching: Preserve the gallery's role of comparing intended poses with animation across movement types. Narrate target/action/result in our version. Avoid copying every silent reference page or substituting only unrelated combat footage.
sections.personalAttribution: The source's approximate 70-80 pages per fighter is a personal production report, not a universal specification requirement.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Use shared licensed characters/props and independently editable Unity shots on one fixed grid. Maintain a pose thumbnail beside the moving realization; include attack, dodge, idle and expressive gesture roles. Actual commercial-game proof must come from separate eligible recordings.
sections.transitionToNext: Visual pose documents work well for many bodies, but the appropriate reference changes when an existing work or an unusual body already defines the movement.

claims: An existing source game's movement can be specified through screenshots when it is the relevant reference.
A strongly nonhumanoid character may be better described in text than forced into a human-shaped figure reference.
sections.observedVisuals: Terry's source-game taunt images compared with Smash animation; Piranha Plant moves on the grid.
exampleRoles: Terry: preserve a recognizable existing movement identity.
Piranha Plant: expose the limits of a humanoid pose reference.
sections.retainedTeaching: Choose the representation that expresses the actual body and action; a figure is a method, not a mandatory template.
sections.ownScreenProposal: One split comparison for an existing-game gesture using independently sourced rights-checked evidence; then a nonhumanoid licensed model whose stem/body movement is specified with short text and a directional curve on our grid.
sections.transitionToNext: These references establish intent, but even a thorough document cannot decide every motion detail.

claims: A detailed planning package is only the first stage of animation production.
Animators must solve many details to make movement coherent and convincing.
An articulated toy's movement range differs from the game model's range, so the photo cannot be reproduced mechanically.
sections.observedVisuals: Inkling squid-run specification versus final movement; figure overlay illustrates physical articulation limits.
sections.retainedTeaching: Keep room for the animator's judgment; do not promise that more specification eliminates iteration or creative work.
additionalPrerequisites: Explain range of motion through one joint and one visibly restricted movement rather than an undefined rigging term.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Hold a target key pose on the grid, then show the connecting motion. Compare a deliberately restricted joint with an approved in-range variant, labeling the demonstration as our rig rather than the behavior of the reference game.
sections.transitionToNext: Because the reference and the moving model differ, review must judge the realized experience and sometimes change the original plan.

claims: Repeated supervision does not guarantee that every planned movement will work.
Some ideas may need to be abandoned or adjusted.
The objective is a better play experience and a character whose identity reads clearly.
sections.observedVisuals: Hero pose specifications compared with airborne jump/fall animation.
sections.retainedTeaching: Review the moving result against the intended experience; the specification is a shared target, not an untouchable drawing.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Return to the same attack or dodge from the opening and compare the first execution with the refined version on the same camera and grid. Note the visible changed body/weapon relationship rather than inventing an official measured improvement.
sections.transitionToNext: The useful discoveries from one review should reach everyone who creates related movements.

claims: Share direction and feedback with the whole animation team.
Common knowledge of production techniques and pitfalls reduces repeated mistakes and grows shared experience.
sections.observedVisuals: Presenter closes with all-animators participation as the process recommendation.
sections.retainedTeaching: Conclude with a shared brief and shared review improving the team, after the specification-to-animation lesson rather than as an unrelated management chapter.
sections.ownScreenProposal: Keep the final grid character moving while the compact motion list, pose reference, review note and shared checklist appear as one connected process.
sections.transitionToNext: End this episode on the completed communication loop; do not append the next episode's technical lesson.
